title: Database Indexing Under the Hood: B+ Trees, Hash Indexes, and GiST Spatial Trees in High-Concurrency Storage Engines
summary: Every database query either scans entire sequential heap tables (O(N) cost) or traverses an index (O(log N) or O(1) cost). However, choosing the wrong index structure introduces severe disk bloat and write degradation without accelerating queries. While B+ Trees remain the default choice for range scans and sorting, specialized structures like Hash Indexes, Generalized Search Trees (GiST), and Generalized Inverted Indexes (GIN) solve multi-dimensional, geometric, and full-text search challenges. Understanding page layout, branching factors, and latch concurrency is key to optimizing analytical and transactional database workloads.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Library Navigation Systems: The Catalog Cards vs. The Map Room
analogy:
Imagine a massive central library with 10 million books stored across 5 floors.

Under Full Table Scan (The Blind Wanderer), a reader looking for a book walks down every single aisle on all five floors, checking book titles one-by-one until finding the target. A single lookup takes five hours.

Under B+ Tree Indexing (The Alphabetical Card Catalog), the reader walks to a filing cabinet labeled A–Z. The first drawer points to drawer 'S–T', which points to cards 'Si–Sm', which gives the exact shelf and slot number. The reader finds the book in 3 steps. The bottom cards are linked with ribbons, so finding all authors between 'Singla' and 'Smith' requires following the ribbon without returning to the main cabinet.

Under GiST Indexing (The Coordinate Map Room), for finding 'all restaurants within 5 miles of central station', alphabetical filing is useless. The map room uses hierarchical bounding boxes (country → city → neighborhood → street) to eliminate 99% of geography instantly.

sections.heading: 1. The Anatomy of a B+ Tree: Why Leaves Are Linked
sections.content:
The B+ Tree is the foundational storage index across relational engines (InnoDB, PostgreSQL, SQLite). Unlike standard binary search trees or standard B-trees, the B+ Tree enforces two critical physical structural invariants:

• All Data Pointers Reside in Leaves: Internal routing nodes store only search keys and child page pointers, maximizing the branching factor. A single 8 KB or 16 KB internal page can store 400 to 500 keys, allowing a 4-level B+ Tree to index hundreds of millions of rows within just 4 disk page lookups.
• Doubly Linked Leaf Level: Leaf pages form a contiguous doubly linked list. When a query executes a range filter (e.g., WHERE age BETWEEN 25 AND 35), the engine performs a single logarithmic search to the first leaf node and then sequentially walks sibling leaf pointers, eliminating tree re-traversals.

sections.heading: 2. When Hash, GiST, and GIN Outperform B+ Trees
sections.content:
Despite the versatility of B+ Trees, specific access patterns demand alternative indexing strategies:

• Hash Indexes (O(1) Exact Equality):
Maintains an array of hash buckets. Ideal strictly for exact equality lookups (WHERE api_key = 'xyz'). Hash indexes cannot perform range scans, prefix matching, or sorted ordering. In modern PostgreSQL, hash indexes are WAL-logged and crash-safe, offering a smaller footprint than B-trees for long string keys.

• GiST (Generalized Search Tree):
An extensible balanced tree structure implementing hierarchical bounding boxes (R-Tree layout). Essential for geometric, spatial (PostGIS), and range types (e.g., timestamp interval overlaps WHERE period && '[2026-10-01, 2026-10-15]').

• GIN (Generalized Inverted Index):
Splits complex composite values (JSONB documents, text arrays, full-text lexemes) into individual elements. GIN maps each unique element to an array of heap tuple IDs. While heavier on writes, GIN accelerates multi-attribute document filters by orders of magnitude.

sections.heading: 3. Index Maintenance Overhead: Write Amplification and Page Splits
sections.content:
Indexes are not free; every additional index on a table exacts a continuous toll on write operations:

• Page Splits and Latch Contention: When an insert targets a leaf page that is 100% full, the engine must allocate a new page, migrate 50% of the tuples, and update parent node pointers. This page split holds exclusive latches, temporarily blocking concurrent reads and writes.
• HOT (Heap-Only Tuples) in PostgreSQL: If an UPDATE statement modifies only non-indexed columns and the new row version fits on the same data page, PostgreSQL avoids updating indexes entirely, reducing WAL volume and preventing index bloat.
• Fill Factor Tuning: For write-heavy tables with frequent updates, reducing the table or index fillfactor (e.g., from 100% to 80%) leaves intentional headroom in each page, drastically reducing page split frequency.

takeaway: Indexes are precise trade-offs between read speed and write amplification. B+ Trees maximize fan-out and provide ultra-fast sequential range scans via doubly linked leaf pages, while specialized Hash, GiST, and GIN indexes accelerate exact keys, spatial bounds, and unstructured JSONB documents.
